newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian rally banned after mass investor protests.
newsitem.headline: Albanian rally banned after mass investor protests.

text.p: Albania's right-wing rulers banned a giant protest rally planned for Saturday by opponents who urged investors duped by pyramid schemes to draw inspiration from protests in Bulgaria and Serbia.
An interior ministry statement, read on state television after three days of anti-government protests in southern Albania, said the rally posed a security risk and was illegal.
Flouting of the law, it said, would be met with "punishments as provided by the criminal code".

Tens of thousands of enraged depositors who poured into streets and squares in the port of Vlore this week pledged to keep protesting until they got their money back and secured the departure of President Sali Berisha's government.
Many saw the shift of the protest at the weekend to the capital as a turning point in their crusade.
"Every day to the square, every day in Vlore, every day in Tirana," shouted the marchers. "Tomorrow in Tirana," others replied in chorus.

"We are calling for mass protests like in other Balkan countries," Kastriot Islami, spokesman for the Socialist Party, the backbone of the Forum for Democracy grouping, told Reuters Television before the ban was imposed.
It was uncertain whether party leaders, their rank and file or weary depositors who lost life savings would defy the order.

Demonstrators set fire to public buildings in several cities last month to denounce the collapse of the schemes and authorities responded by arresting more than 150 and threatening them with long jail sentences.
That was enough to keep streets all but clear of demonstrators in Tirana and other cities last weekend.
Protests in Vlore, sparked by the folding last week of the Gjallica investment scheme popular in the region, were largely impromptu affairs.
After outwitting and outnumbering police cordons on the first day, women and children paraded alongside their menfolk up and down the town's main palm-lined boulevard to the port.
Politicians made their first appearance on Friday night.
"These people want change, not just their money," said Neritan Ceka, head of the centre-right Democratic Alliance. "Tonight's rally amounts to approval (for Saturday's protest)."
Out of sight since chairing cross-party talks on the failed schemes on Tuesday, Berisha has made no comment on the rallies.
But his Democratic Party, in a statement also broadcast on television, urged Albanians to "assess with a clear mind the red terror organised by the Socialist Party.
"The Democratic Party calls on all citizens not to blindly follow forces aiming to create a drama many times worse than that of the pyramid schemes," it said.

Berisha's Democrats won re-election last year in polls criticised as unfair by Western observers. Some opposition politicians accuse the party of financing the victory with proceeds from the failed investment companies.

The schemes, which initially fulfilled promises of high, regular interest payments,have drawn savings from virtually every Albanian family in the six years since the fall of hardline communists, the most repressive in eastern Europe.
Economists believe up to $2 billion may have been tied up in the plans. Depositors in two bankrupt companies began receiving partial refunds this week but bankers say the payouts could take months.
